items.title: Ecosystem, Energy Flow & Ecological Pyramids
items.body:
### Ecosystem, energy flow and ecological pyramids

**In one line**
An ecosystem is living things plus their surroundings working as one unit, and energy moves through it in only one direction, shrinking at every step.

**Why it is asked**
The 10% law, the "which pyramid can invert" question, and grazing-vs-detritus food chains are repeat favourites.

**The story**
An **ecosystem** is a working unit where **biotic** parts (living: producers, consumers, decomposers) interact with **abiotic** parts (non-living: light, water, soil, temperature). **Producers** (green plants) capture sunlight; **consumers** eat others — primary (herbivores), then secondary and tertiary; **decomposers** break down the dead and recycle nutrients. Energy passes along a **food chain** through steps called **trophic levels**, and many chains linked together form a more stable **food web**. The crucial rule is **Lindeman's 10% law**: only about **10% of the energy at one level reaches the next** — the rest is lost as heat and in respiration. Because so much is lost, chains rarely run beyond **4-5 links**. This loss also shapes **ecological pyramids**: the **pyramid of energy is always upright** (energy only shrinks upward), while pyramids of **number** and **biomass can sometimes be inverted** (for example, one big tree feeding many insects, or few large fish supported by vast tiny plankton in a pond).

**Picture it**

| Pyramid | Usually | Can it invert? |
|---|---|---|
| Number | Upright | Yes (a tree, or parasites) |
| Biomass | Upright | Yes (aquatic/pond) |
| Energy | Upright | Never (10% law) |

**Terms explained**
- **Biotic / abiotic** = living parts / non-living parts of an ecosystem.
- **Trophic level** = a feeding step (producer, herbivore, carnivore).
- **Grazing food chain** = starts with living green plants.
- **Detritus food chain** = starts with dead organic matter.

**Don't confuse**
- **Only the energy pyramid can never invert.** Number and biomass pyramids can.
- Energy flow is **one-way (unidirectional)**; it does not cycle back like nutrients do.

**Remember it**
"Energy only falls, and only 10% survives each step — so the energy pyramid stands tall."

**TL;DR**
- Ecosystem = biotic + abiotic parts interacting as one unit.
- Energy flow is one-way; the 10% law passes only ~10% upward.
- Grazing chain starts with green plants; detritus chain with dead matter.
- Pyramid of energy is always upright; number and biomass pyramids can invert.
keyPoints: Ecosystem = biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) + abiotic components interacting as a functional unit.
Energy flow is unidirectional; Lindeman's 10% law passes only ~10% of energy to the next trophic level.
Grazing food chain starts with green plants; detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter.
Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright; pyramids of number and biomass can be inverted.
Food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic links because of energy loss.

items.title: Biodiversity, Hotspots & India's Megadiversity
items.body:
### Biodiversity, hotspots and India's megadiversity

**In one line**
Biodiversity is the variety of life at three levels, and a "hotspot" is a region that is both exceptionally rich and badly threatened — India has four.

**Why it is asked**
The three levels, the "17 megadiverse / ~2.4% land, ~8% species" statistic, and the two-part hotspot definition are standard statement-based facts.

**The story**
**Biodiversity** comes in three levels: **genetic** (variety within a species), **species** (variety of different species), and **ecosystem** (variety of habitats). India is **one of 17 megadiverse countries** — with only about **2.4% of the world's land area** it holds roughly **8% of all recorded global biodiversity**. Some regions matter more than others. A **biodiversity hotspot**, as defined by Norman Myers, must pass **two tests together**: it must have at least **1,500 endemic (found-nowhere-else) vascular plant species**, AND it must have already **lost at least 70% of its original (primary) vegetation** — so it is both rich and under threat. **Four hotspots reach into India**: the **Himalaya**, the **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka**, **Indo-Burma** (covering the North-East), and **Sundaland** (the Nicobar Islands).

**Picture it**

| Hotspot | Coverage in India |
|---|---|
| Himalaya | The Indian Himalayan region |
| Western Ghats & Sri Lanka | Western coastal ranges |
| Indo-Burma | North-East India (excluding the Ghats) |
| Sundaland | Nicobar Islands |

**Terms explained**
- **Endemic** = found naturally in one place and nowhere else.
- **Vascular plant** = a plant with water-conducting tissue (most land plants).
- **Megadiverse country** = one of 17 nations holding most of Earth's species.
- **Primary vegetation** = the original, undisturbed natural plant cover.

**Don't confuse**
- A hotspot needs **both** conditions (endemism AND 70% habitat loss), not either one alone.
- "Megadiverse" (a country) is not the same as a "hotspot" (a region).

**Remember it**
"Hotspot = Rich (1,500 endemic plants) + Robbed (70% lost)." India has four.

**TL;DR**
- Three levels of biodiversity: genetic, species, ecosystem.
- India is one of 17 megadiverse countries; ~2.4% land holds ~8% of global biodiversity.
- Hotspot (Myers) = ≥1,500 endemic plants AND ≥70% primary vegetation lost.
- Four hotspots touch India: Himalaya, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Sundaland (Nicobar).
keyPoints: Three levels of biodiversity: genetic, species and ecosystem.
India is one of 17 megadiverse countries; ~2.4% land area holds ~8% of global recorded biodiversity.
A biodiversity hotspot needs >=1,500 endemic plant species AND >=70% loss of primary vegetation (Myers).
Four hotspots touch India: Himalaya, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland (Nicobar).
Western Ghats and North-East (Indo-Burma) are the most biodiverse Indian regions.

items.title: Environmental Legal Framework of India
items.body:
### India's environmental legal framework

**In one line**
A stack of laws protects India's environment, with the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 as the "umbrella" over all of them.

**Why it is asked**
Act-to-year matching, the "umbrella law" tag, and recent renames/amendments (Forest Act 2023, WPA 2022) are frequent one-markers.

**The story**
India built its environmental law piece by piece. The **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** created protected areas and species schedules. The **Water Act, 1974** set up the **Central and State Pollution Control Boards (CPCB/SPCBs)**. The **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980** curbed the diversion of forest land, and the **Air Act, 1981** tackled air pollution. After the **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)**, the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** was passed as the **umbrella law** — it empowers the Centre to take *any* measure to protect the environment and is the parent of rules like the EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) notifications; it also gives effect to the **Stockholm Conference of 1972**. Later came the **Biological Diversity Act, 2002** (creating the National Biodiversity Authority, State Boards and local committees) and the **National Green Tribunal Act, 2010** (a fast-track green court). Recent updates: the WPA was **amended in 2022** to just **four schedules**; the Forest Act was **renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023**; and the Biological Diversity Act was **amended in 2023**.

**Picture it**

| Act | Year | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Wildlife (Protection) Act | 1972 | Protected areas, species schedules |
| Water Act | 1974 | Created CPCB/SPCBs |
| Forest (Conservation) Act | 1980 | Curbs forest-land diversion |
| Air Act | 1981 | Air pollution control |
| Environment (Protection) Act | 1986 | Umbrella law (post-Bhopal) |
| Biological Diversity Act | 2002 | NBA, SBBs, BMCs |
| National Green Tribunal Act | 2010 | Green court |

**Terms explained**
- **Umbrella law** = a broad parent Act under which many specific rules are issued.
- **EIA** = Environmental Impact Assessment, a study before clearing a project.
- **NBA** = National Biodiversity Authority (at Chennai).
- **NGT** = National Green Tribunal (principal bench, New Delhi).

**Don't confuse**
- The **CPCB was created by the Water Act (1974)**, not the EPA.
- The **NGT came from a separate 2010 Act**, not from the EPA 1986.

**Remember it**
"Bhopal 1984 → EPA 1986, the umbrella." Water (1974) made the pollution boards.

**TL;DR**
- EPA 1986 is the umbrella law, enacted after Bhopal (1984), giving effect to Stockholm 1972.
- Water Act (1974) created CPCB/SPCBs; Air Act 1981; NGT Act 2010.
- WPA 1972 amended in 2022 to four schedules.
- Forest Act 1980 renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam (2023); Biological Diversity Act 2002 (NBA, Chennai), amended 2023.
keyPoints: EPA 1986 is the umbrella environmental law, enacted after the 1984 Bhopal tragedy and giving effect to Stockholm 1972.
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 was amended in 2022 to just four schedules.
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 was renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam by the 2023 amendment.
Biological Diversity Act 2002 created the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), SBBs and BMCs; amended 2023.
Water Act (1974) created CPCB/SPCBs; NGT Act 2010 established the National Green Tribunal (principal bench, Delhi).

items.title: Protected Areas & Wildlife Conservation
items.body:
### Protected areas and wildlife conservation

**In one line**
India protects wildlife through four kinds of protected area and a set of flagship species projects, backed by the latest forest and tiger data.

**Why it is asked**
The National-Park-vs-Sanctuary rights distinction, the species-project years, and ISFR 2023 figures are high-yield facts.

**The story**
The **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** sets up four protected-area types with different levels of control. A **National Park** has the **highest protection — no rights and no grazing** are allowed. A **Wildlife Sanctuary** is slightly more relaxed — certain **regulated rights** may be permitted. A **Conservation Reserve** is government land next to a park or sanctuary, managed with the community, and a **Community Reserve** is private or community land that people volunteer to conserve. India's network has grown to about **900 protected areas** — roughly **106 national parks, 573 wildlife sanctuaries, 123 conservation reserves and 86 community reserves**, covering about **5.3% of the country's area**. Flagship **species projects** anchor recovery: **Project Tiger (1973)**, now run by the **NTCA (2005)**; **Project Elephant (1992)**; and **Project Cheetah (2022)**, which brought African cheetahs to **Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh**. India has **58 tiger reserves** and a wild tiger population of **3,682 (2022 census, about 70% of the world's)**. The **India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023** records forest cover at **21.76%** and forest-plus-tree cover at **25.17%** of the geographical area, with mangroves at **4,991.68 km2** (West Bengal's Sundarbans the largest).

**Picture it**

| Project | Year | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Project Tiger | 1973 | NTCA (2005) |
| Project Elephant | 1992 | MoEFCC |
| Project Cheetah | 2022 | Kuno NP (MP) |

**Terms explained**
- **National Park** = strictest protected area; no private rights or grazing.
- **Wildlife Sanctuary** = protected area where some regulated rights may continue.
- **NTCA** = National Tiger Conservation Authority, the statutory tiger body.
- **ISFR** = India State of Forest Report, the biennial forest-cover survey.

**Don't confuse**
- **National Park = no rights; Sanctuary = some regulated rights.** This is the key WPA distinction.
- **Forest cover (21.76%)** is less than **forest + tree cover (25.17%)** — quote the right one.

**Remember it**
"Park = strictest; Project Tiger 1973, NTCA 2005, Cheetah 2022 at Kuno."

**TL;DR**
- Four PA types: National Park, Wildlife Sanctuary, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve.
- Network ~900 PAs (~106 NPs, 573 WLS) covering ~5.3% of area.
- Project Tiger 1973 (NTCA 2005), Project Elephant 1992, Project Cheetah 2022 (Kuno); 58 tiger reserves, 3,682 tigers (2022).
- ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76%, forest+tree 25.17%; mangroves 4,991.68 km2 (WB largest).
keyPoints: National Park allows no rights/grazing; a sanctuary may permit regulated rights (key WPA distinction).
Conservation reserves are govt land near PAs; community reserves are private/community conserved land.
Project Tiger began 1973; NTCA created 2005; India has 58 tiger reserves (2025) with 3,682 tigers (2022).
Project Elephant 1992; Project Cheetah 2022 reintroduced African cheetahs at Kuno NP, Madhya Pradesh.
ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76% and forest+tree cover 25.17% of geographical area; mangroves 4,991.68 km2 (WB largest, the Sundarbans).

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — Protected Areas & Wetlands
items.body:
### Andhra Pradesh — protected areas and wetlands

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh holds India's largest tiger reserve, a famous mangrove sanctuary, and a cluster of important lakes and hill forests.

**Why it is asked**
"Which is AP's only Ramsar site", "largest tiger reserve", and Coringa/Pulicat facts are repeatedly tested, singly and as match-the-list.

**The story**
Andhra Pradesh's crown jewel is the **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR)** in the **Nallamala hills** — the **largest tiger reserve in India**, shared with Telangana. Its national parks are **Papikonda** (on the Godavari, Eastern Ghats) and **Sri Venkateswara** (the Tirupati/Seshachalam hills). Along the coast, the **Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary** in the Godavari estuary near Kakinada is India's **second-largest mangrove** formation (after the Sundarbans). **Pulicat Lake**, shared with Tamil Nadu, is India's **second-largest brackish-water lagoon** (after Chilika), with the **Nelapattu** pelican sanctuary nearby. **Kolleru Lake**, between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, is one of India's largest freshwater lakes and **AP's only Ramsar site** (designated 2002). **Rollapadu Wildlife Sanctuary** protects the **Great Indian Bustard**, and the **Seshachalam** hills (red-sanders forest) form AP's **biosphere reserve (2010)**.

**Picture it**

| Area | Type | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam | Tiger Reserve | Largest in India (Nallamala) |
| Coringa | Wildlife Sanctuary | 2nd-largest mangrove in India |
| Pulicat | Lagoon/sanctuary | 2nd-largest brackish lagoon |
| Kolleru | Freshwater lake | AP's only Ramsar site (2002) |
| Seshachalam | Biosphere reserve | Red-sanders forest (2010) |

**Terms explained**
- **Brackish water** = water saltier than fresh but less salty than the sea.
- **Estuary** = where a river's mouth meets the sea, mixing fresh and salt water.
- **Ramsar site** = a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention.
- **Mangrove** = salt-tolerant coastal forest that shields the shore.

**Don't confuse**
- **Kolleru (freshwater) is AP's Ramsar site; Pulicat is a brackish lagoon**, not the Ramsar site.
- **Coringa = 2nd-largest mangrove; Pulicat = 2nd-largest brackish lagoon** — different "second-largest" titles.

**Remember it**
"NSTR biggest tiger, Coringa the mangrove, Kolleru the Ramsar lake, Seshachalam the biosphere."

**TL;DR**
- Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam = India's largest tiger reserve (Nallamala, shared with Telangana).
- Coringa = India's 2nd-largest mangrove; Pulicat = 2nd-largest brackish lagoon.
- Kolleru = AP's only Ramsar site (2002); Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara are AP national parks.
- Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; Rollapadu protects the Great Indian Bustard.
keyPoints: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve is the LARGEST tiger reserve in India (Nallamala hills), shared with Telangana.
Coringa WLS (Godavari estuary) is India's second-largest mangrove formation after the Sundarbans.
Pulicat Lake is India's second-largest brackish-water lagoon (after Chilika), on the AP-Tamil Nadu border.
Kolleru Lake is AP's only Ramsar site (designated 2002); Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara are AP national parks.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; Rollapadu WLS protects the Great Indian Bustard.

items.title: Wetlands, Biosphere Reserves & Species Conventions
items.body:
### Wetlands, biosphere reserves and species conventions

**In one line**
A set of global agreements protects wetlands (Ramsar), model ecosystems (UNESCO biosphere reserves) and threatened or traded species (CITES, CMS, CBD).

**Why it is asked**
Ramsar's year/place, India's site count and "most in Tamil Nadu", the first biosphere reserve, and convention-to-focus matching are reliable facts.

**The story**
The **Ramsar Convention on Wetlands** was signed in **1971 at Ramsar, Iran**, to conserve wetlands and promote their **"wise use"**. **India joined in 1982** and now has **101 Ramsar sites (as of August 2026)** — the **most are in Tamil Nadu**. The **Montreux Record** is a watch-list of Ramsar sites facing harmful ecological change (India's are **Keoladeo** and **Loktak**). Separately, **biosphere reserves** are designated under **UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme (1971)** and zoned into **core, buffer and transition** areas; India has **18 biosphere reserves**, of which **Nilgiri (1986)** was the first and **12** are on the UNESCO **World Network (WNBR)** — AP's is **Seshachalam (2010)**. For species, four instruments recur: the **IUCN Red List** rates conservation status; **CITES (1973)** controls trade in endangered species; **CMS/Bonn (1979)** protects migratory species (India hosted **COP13 at Gandhinagar in 2020**); and the **CBD (Rio, 1992)** covers biodiversity, with its **Cartagena** (biosafety) and **Nagoya** (benefit-sharing) protocols.

**Picture it**

| Body | Focus |
|---|---|
| IUCN Red List | Conservation status (CR/EN/VU...) |
| CITES (1973) | Trade in endangered species |
| CMS / Bonn (1979) | Migratory species |
| CBD (1992) | Biodiversity; Cartagena & Nagoya protocols |

**Terms explained**
- **Wise use** = sustainable use of wetlands without destroying them.
- **Montreux Record** = Ramsar's list of threatened wetland sites.
- **MAB zones** = core (strictly protected), buffer, transition (human activity allowed).
- **CITES Appendices** = lists I-III ranking trade restrictions by threat level.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ramsar (wetlands) is NOT a UNESCO body** — biosphere reserves are the UNESCO (MAB) ones.
- **CITES = trade; CMS = migration; IUCN Red List = status; CBD = diversity.**

**Remember it**
"Ramsar 1971 Iran; Nilgiri 1986 first biosphere; CITES trades, CMS migrates."

**TL;DR**
- Ramsar Convention signed 1971 (Ramsar, Iran); India joined 1982, has 101 sites (2026), most in Tamil Nadu.
- Montreux Record flags threatened sites (Keoladeo, Loktak).
- Biosphere reserves under UNESCO MAB (1971): India has 18, Nilgiri (1986) first, 12 on WNBR; Seshachalam (2010) in AP.
- CITES (1973) trade, CMS/Bonn (1979) migratory, CBD (1992) biodiversity (Cartagena, Nagoya).
keyPoints: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; India joined in 1982 and has 101 sites (2026).
Tamil Nadu has the most Ramsar sites in India; the Montreux Record flags threatened sites (Keoladeo, Loktak).
Biosphere reserves follow UNESCO MAB (1971) with core/buffer/transition zones; India has 18, Nilgiri (1986) first.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; 12 Indian reserves are on the UNESCO World Network (WNBR).
CITES (1973) regulates trade; CMS/Bonn (1979) covers migratory species (India hosted CMS COP13, Gandhinagar 2020); CBD (Rio 1992) has the Cartagena and Nagoya protocols.

items.title: Climate Change & the International Framework
items.body:
### Climate change and the international framework

**In one line**
Greenhouse gases warm the planet, the IPCC assesses the science, and a chain of treaties from the UNFCCC to the Paris Agreement coordinates the global response.

**Why it is asked**
GHG identification, IPCC parentage, the UNFCCC-Kyoto-Paris timeline, and recent-COP facts (Loss and Damage, Belem) are directly examinable.

**The story**
**Greenhouse gases (GHGs)** — carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapour, ozone, CFCs and **sulphur hexafluoride (SF6, the highest global-warming potential)** — trap outgoing heat and drive **global warming**. The **IPCC**, set up jointly by the **WMO and UNEP in 1988**, *assesses* (does not conduct) climate science; its **Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2021-23)** warns warming will likely cross **1.5 degrees C** in the near term. The treaty chain begins with the **UNFCCC (Rio, 1992)**, the parent framework built on **"common but differentiated responsibilities"**. The **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** set **binding targets on developed nations** and used market mechanisms. The **Paris Agreement (2015, COP21)** asks all countries to hold warming **well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C** through self-set **Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)** and net-zero goals. Recent conferences: **COP27 (2022, Sharm el-Sheikh)** created the **Loss and Damage Fund**; **COP28 (2023, Dubai)** held the first **Global Stocktake** and called to "transition away from fossil fuels"; **COP29 (2024, Baku)** set a new climate-finance goal; and **COP30 (November 2025, Belem, Brazil)** in the Amazon focused on implementation and forests.

**Picture it**

| Instrument | Year | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| UNFCCC | 1992 | Parent framework; CBDR |
| Kyoto Protocol | 1997 | Binding targets on developed nations |
| Paris Agreement | 2015 | Well below 2 C, pursue 1.5 C; NDCs |

**Terms explained**
- **GHG** = greenhouse gas, which traps heat in the atmosphere.
- **CBDR** = common but differentiated responsibilities (richer, higher-emitting nations do more).
- **NDC** = Nationally Determined Contribution, each country's self-set climate pledge.
- **Global Stocktake** = a periodic review of collective progress under Paris.

**Don't confuse**
- **The IPCC assesses science; it does not run experiments or set targets.**
- **UNFCCC (1992) is the parent; Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015)** sit under it — keep the order.

**Remember it**
"Rio 1992 (UNFCCC) → Kyoto 1997 → Paris 2015." Loss & Damage = COP27 (2022).

**TL;DR**
- Main GHGs: CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, ozone, CFCs, SF6 (highest GWP).
- IPCC (WMO+UNEP, 1988); AR6 warns of crossing 1.5 C in the near term.
- UNFCCC (1992) parent; Kyoto (1997) binding on developed nations; Paris (2015) well below 2 C via NDCs.
- Loss and Damage Fund at COP27 (2022); COP28 (2023) first Global Stocktake; COP30 at Belem (Nov 2025).
keyPoints: Main GHGs: CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, ozone, CFCs and SF6 (highest global-warming potential).
IPCC (WMO+UNEP, 1988) AR6 (2021-23) warns warming will likely cross 1.5 C in the near term.
UNFCCC (Rio 1992) is the parent treaty; Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding targets on developed nations.
Paris Agreement (2015, COP21) aims to hold warming well below 2 C (pursue 1.5 C) via nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
Loss and Damage Fund was agreed at COP27 (2022); COP28 (2023) held the first Global Stocktake; COP30 was held at Belem, Brazil (Nov 2025).

items.title: India's Climate Action, NAPCC & Pollution Control
items.body:
### India's climate action, NAPCC and pollution control

**In one line**
India backs its net-zero-by-2070 pledge with five quantified targets (Panchamrit), eight national missions (NAPCC), a lifestyle movement (Mission LiFE) and pollution/disaster laws.

**Why it is asked**
The five Panchamrit numbers, the "eight missions" count, Mission LiFE, and the DM Act/NDMA chain are frequent single-fact and match items.

**The story**
At **COP26 (Glasgow, 2021)** India announced **Panchamrit** (five nectars): **500 GW** non-fossil capacity by 2030, **50%** of energy from renewables by 2030, cutting **1 billion tonnes** of CO2 by 2030, reducing the **emissions intensity of GDP by 45%** by 2030, and **net-zero by 2070**. The policy engine is the **National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008)** with **eight missions** — Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, and Strategic Knowledge — mirrored by **State Action Plans (SAPCCs)**. India also leads a demand-side movement, **Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment, 2022)**, urging "Pro Planet People" behaviour, and two India-initiated coalitions, the **International Solar Alliance (ISA)** and the **Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI)**. On pollution and disasters, the **National Clean Air Programme (NCAP, 2019)** targets particulate cuts (tracked via the six-band **AQI**); **single-use plastics were banned from 1 July 2022**; and the **Disaster Management Act, 2005** created the **NDMA (chaired by the PM)**, SDMAs and the **NDRF**, with India following the global **Sendai Framework (2015-30)** — vital for AP's cyclone-prone coast.

**Picture it**

| Panchamrit target (by 2030) | Figure |
|---|---|
| Non-fossil capacity | 500 GW |
| Energy from renewables | 50% |
| CO2 reduction | 1 billion tonnes |
| Emissions intensity of GDP | down 45% |
| Net-zero | by 2070 |

**Terms explained**
- **Net-zero** = balancing emissions released with emissions removed.
- **Emissions intensity** = emissions per unit of GDP, not total emissions.
- **AQI** = Air Quality Index, with six bands from Good to Severe.
- **NDMA/NDRF** = National Disaster Management Authority / National Disaster Response Force.

**Don't confuse**
- **Net-zero is 2070, but the other four Panchamrit targets are for 2030.**
- **Mission LiFE is a behaviour movement, not a NAPCC mission.**

**Remember it**
"5 nectars: 500 GW, 50%, 1 bn t, 45% less intensity, net-zero 2070." NAPCC = 8 missions.

**TL;DR**
- Panchamrit (COP26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil, 50% renewables, cut 1 bn t CO2, -45% emissions intensity (all 2030), net-zero 2070.
- NAPCC (2008) has eight missions; states have SAPCCs.
- Mission LiFE (2022) is India's pro-planet lifestyle push; ISA and CDRI are India-initiated.
- NCAP (2019) + AQI; single-use plastic banned 1 July 2022; DM Act 2005 (NDMA/NDRF), Sendai 2015-30.
keyPoints: Panchamrit (COP26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil by 2030, 50% renewables, cut 1 bn t CO2, -45% emissions intensity, net-zero by 2070.
NAPCC (2008) has eight missions incl. Solar, Energy Efficiency, Green India, Water and Himalayan Ecosystem; states have SAPCCs.
Mission LiFE (2022) is India's pro-planet lifestyle initiative; ISA and CDRI are India-initiated global coalitions.
National Clean Air Programme (2019) uses AQI (6 bands); single-use plastic banned from 1 July 2022.
Disaster Management Act 2005 created NDMA (chaired by PM) and NDRF; India follows the Sendai Framework 2015-30.

items.title: Pollution, Climate Concepts & Ecology — Exam Fact Cluster
items.body:
### Pollution, climate concepts and ecology — exam fact cluster

**In one line**
This note bundles the tricky one-fact items APPSC loves: geoengineering, carbon fertilization, pollution chemistry, fertiliser effects and ecology traps.

**Why it is asked**
Each cluster matches a real statement-based MCQ, where one wrong word (e.g. "nanoparticles do not exist in nature") flips the answer.

**The story**
Some ideas appear again and again. **Geoengineering / Solar Radiation Management (SRM)** — such as injecting **sulphate aerosols** into the stratosphere or **thinning cirrus clouds** — is proposed to **reduce global warming** by reflecting or releasing heat. **Carbon fertilization** means **extra plant growth caused by higher atmospheric CO2**. **Remote sensing** can measure **chlorophyll in vegetation, greenhouse-gas emissions from rice paddies, and land-surface temperature**. **Neem-coated urea** is promoted because it **slows urea's dissolution in soil**, raising nitrogen-use efficiency. In pollution chemistry, **acid rain** comes from **SO2 and NOx** forming sulphuric and nitric acid; **photochemical smog** needs **NOx + VOCs + sunlight**, producing ozone and **PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate)**; and **eutrophication** is nutrient (N, P) over-enrichment of water. **Excess nitrogen fertiliser** raises **soil acidity** and **leaches nitrate into groundwater** (it does **not** boost nitrogen-fixing microbes). **Bisphenol A (BPA)** is a component of **polycarbonate** plastic and an **endocrine disruptor**; **benzene** is a VOC from exhaust, tobacco and wood. In ecology, **decomposers are fungi and bacteria** (not viruses); common **mutualisms** include coral-zooxanthellae and lichen (fungus + alga); and a classification trap: the **sea cow and sea lion are mammals**, but the **sea horse is a fish**.

**Picture it**

| Phenomenon | Cause |
|---|---|
| Acid rain | SO2 + NOx |
| Photochemical smog | NOx + VOCs + sunlight (gives O3, PAN) |
| Eutrophication | Nutrient (N, P) enrichment of water |

**Terms explained**
- **SRM** = solar radiation management, reflecting sunlight to cool the planet.
- **VOC** = volatile organic compound (e.g. benzene).
- **Endocrine disruptor** = a chemical that interferes with hormones.
- **Decomposer** = an organism (fungi, bacteria) that breaks down dead matter.

**Don't confuse**
- **Natural nanoparticles DO exist** (soot, volcanic ash) — "only human-made" is false.
- **Excess N fertiliser suppresses, not multiplies, N-fixing microbes.**
- **Sea horse is a fish**, not a mammal.

**Remember it**
"Acid rain = S + N; smog = N + VOC + sun; sea horse = fish." BPA = polycarbonate.

**TL;DR**
- SRM (sulphate aerosols, cirrus thinning) aims to reduce warming; carbon fertilization = CO2-driven plant growth.
- Remote sensing measures chlorophyll, paddy GHGs, land-surface temperature; neem-coated urea slows urea release.
- Acid rain = SO2 + NOx; photochemical smog = NOx + VOC + sunlight (O3, PAN); excess N fertiliser acidifies soil and leaches nitrate.
- Decomposers are fungi/bacteria; sea cow and sea lion are mammals, sea horse is a fish; BPA is an endocrine disruptor.
keyPoints: Sulphate-aerosol injection and cirrus-cloud thinning are geoengineering methods to reduce global warming.
Carbon fertilization = higher plant growth due to increased atmospheric CO2.
Remote sensing can measure chlorophyll, paddy GHG emissions and land-surface temperature.
Neem-coated urea slows urea dissolution in soil, improving nitrogen-use efficiency.
Acid rain is caused by SO2 and NOx; photochemical smog needs NOx + VOCs + sunlight, forming O3 and PAN.
Excess nitrogenous fertilizer increases soil acidity and leaches nitrate to groundwater.
BPA is a component of polycarbonate plastic and an endocrine disruptor; benzene is a VOC from exhaust/tobacco/wood.
Decomposers are fungi and bacteria (not viruses); sea cow and sea lion are mammals while sea horse is a fish.

items.title: For Mains — Environment, Biodiversity & Climate Change
items.body:
### For Mains — Environment, biodiversity and climate change

**In one line**
For Paper-5, argue the development-versus-environment balance using India's climate pledges, conservation framework and nature-based coastal resilience.

**Why it is asked**
The syllabus clauses cover "development vs environment; pollution; climate change; natural disasters" and "environmental legislation (Montreal/Kyoto/CITES/COP21); SDGs", so answers must weigh growth against sustainability.

**The story**
Mains questions ask you to **evaluate and prescribe** — India's climate commitments, biodiversity-conservation gaps, or wetland and disaster resilience. Build around dimensions and quote dated instruments.

**Picture it**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Problem | Climate change, pollution, biodiversity loss, disasters |
| Commitments | Panchamrit (COP26), net-zero 2070, NDCs, SDGs |
| Framework | EPA 1986, WPA 1972, Forest Act (2023), NAPCC's 8 missions, NGT |
| Conventions | UNFCCC/Kyoto/Paris, CBD/Cartagena/Nagoya, Ramsar, CITES |
| Limitations | Forest diversion, man-animal conflict, finance gaps, enforcement |
| Way forward | Nature-based solutions, CAMPA funding, community participation, One Health |

**Facts to quote**
- Panchamrit: **500 GW** non-fossil, net-zero **2070**; India leads **ISA** and **CDRI**.
- **101 Ramsar sites (2026)**; **58 tiger reserves**; ISFR 2023 forest+tree cover **25.17%**.
- **COP30 (Belem, Nov 2025)**; Loss and Damage Fund (COP27, 2022).
- AP angle: **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam** (largest tiger reserve), **Coringa** mangroves (AP had the largest mangrove increase in ISFR 2023), **Kolleru** Ramsar site, cyclone resilience under the **DM Act 2005 / Sendai**.

**Terms explained**
- **Blue carbon** = carbon captured by coastal ecosystems like mangroves.
- **Nature-based solution** = using ecosystems (mangroves, wetlands) to solve problems like flooding.

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite mangrove bio-shields and the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone for disaster resilience.
- Quote: India's "net-zero by 2070" pledge to frame climate ambition versus equity.
- Diagram idea: a see-saw balancing "development" against "environment", stabilised by sustainability.

**TL;DR**
- Frame as development vs environment, backed by SDGs and net-zero 2070.
- Anchor with EPA 1986, NAPCC's 8 missions, Paris Agreement and Ramsar/CITES.
- Quote 101 Ramsar sites, 58 tiger reserves, ISFR 2023, COP30 Belem 2025.
- Bring the AP angle: NSTR, Coringa mangroves, Kolleru, cyclone resilience.
keyPoints: Mains (Paper-5) asks you to balance development vs environment, backed by SDGs and net-zero 2070.
Climate: Panchamrit (COP26) — 500 GW non-fossil, net-zero 2070; India leads ISA and CDRI; COP30 at Belem (2025).
Framework to quote: EPA 1986, WPA 1972, Forest Act (renamed 2023), NAPCC's 8 missions, NGT 2010.
Conservation data: 101 Ramsar sites (2026), 58 tiger reserves, ISFR 2023 forest+tree cover 25.17%.
AP angle: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (largest tiger reserve), Coringa mangroves, Kolleru Ramsar site, cyclone resilience (DM Act 2005, Sendai).
Way forward: nature-based solutions, CAMPA funding, community participation and One Health.
